title: Vows
hookLine: monks and nuns vow poverty, chastity and obedience, or stability

lines: A PAPER LAID ON THE ALTAR.
UPHOLD ME, THAT I MAY LIVE.
cards: A man in a plain black habit stands at the altar of a monastery church. In front of his brothers, he signs a sheet of paper he has written out by hand and lays it on the altar.
Then he lifts his arms and sings a single line from the Psalms, asking God to uphold him so that he may live, and not be put to shame in his hope. The monks sing it back, and again.
Then he lies down on the floor while they pray. When he gets up, he belongs to that community for good. Today: vows.

teach.h: SELL THAT THOU HAST, AND FOLLOW.
teach.b: A vow is a promise made to God, out loud, meant to be kept, and some Christians make vows that shape their whole lives. Start with a story.

In Matthew, a rich young man asks Jesus what he still lacks, and Jesus answers: "If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come and follow me."

The young man goes away sorrowful. But according to his biographer Athanasius, a young Egyptian named Antony heard that same verse read in church, gave away his land, and began a life of prayer. Next, what they vow.
In Catholic religious life the classic vows are poverty, chastity and obedience: owning nothing of your own, not marrying, and listening for God's will through the community and its leaders.
Benedictines, following the Rule of Saint Benedict, vow stability, staying with one community; conversion of life; and obedience. Stability means no running away when the brothers get on your nerves.
Orthodox monks and nuns make vows too, and so do some Anglican and Lutheran communities. Then, how seriously.

teach.h: BETTER NOT TO VOW THAN NOT PAY.
teach.b: Ecclesiastes warns: "Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay." Communities go slowly too, testing someone a long time before the final vow. Last, how publicly.
A psalm says, "I will pay my vows unto the LORD now in the presence of all his people." The paper on the altar says the same. Not a private resolution.
A whole life, given wholly, with witnesses.

how: Catholic monks, nuns, friars and sisters profess vows such as poverty, chastity and obedience, and Benedictines vow stability, conversion of life and obedience, after a long period of testing; Orthodox monastics and some Anglican and Lutheran communities also take vows.

games.q: you're a young man in Egypt named Antony, sitting in church, and you hear Jesus's words read aloud: "go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor." what do you do?
o: admire the verse and go home as before.
give away your land and begin a life of prayer.
ask the priest whether it applies to you.
games.why: according to Athanasius, Antony went out, gave away his land, and began a life of prayer: the verse the rich young man walked away from.

practice: Make one vow small enough to keep, for today only: no phone at dinner, or one kind word to someone who irritates you. Say it once, quietly, out loud, so it's a promise and not just a thought.
If you pray, make it to God; if you don't, make it to yourself, with this minute as your witness.

wordCard.voice: Vows. Promises made to God out loud before witnesses, like poverty, chastity and obedience, or stability: a life given over on purpose.

orig.note: Hebrew: a vow, the noun Ecclesiastes uses just before its warning about vowing and not paying.

carryVoice: Your line: given wholly. Kept for a day, or kept for life. That's today, done.
